text: Right now, your head is older than your feet.
Not by much. Over an entire lifetime, the difference adds up to less than a tenth of a millionth of a second.
But it's real. It has been measured. And the experiments that measured it are some of the strangest things humans have ever done.
We raced particles down a mountain. We bought plane tickets for clocks. We lifted a clock by the height of two stair steps… and then we did something even more absurd.
Four experiments. Each one smaller than the last. And by the end, time won't be the thing you thought it was.
Every second, particles from deep space slam into the top of our atmosphere. The collisions set off showers of debris — and some of that debris is a particle called the muon.
A muon is like a heavier cousin of the electron, with one big problem: it doesn't last. On average, a muon falls apart in about two millionths of a second.
And muons are born high up — many kilometers above our heads. Even moving at nearly the speed of light, most of them should decay long before they reach the ground.
And yet, detectors at sea level catch them all the time.

In the early 1960s, two physicists, David Frisch and James Smith, decided to count them properly. They hauled a detector to the summit of Mount Washington in New Hampshire — almost two kilometers up — and counted muons moving at one specific speed.
Then they brought the detector down to sea level, in Cambridge, Massachusetts, and counted again.
The math looked simple. Given how long a muon lives, and how long the trip down the mountain takes, then for every 568 muons at the top, only about 27 should have survived to the bottom.
They counted 412.
Fifteen times more than expected.

The only explanation that fits is Einstein's. For a particle moving at more than ninety-nine percent of the speed of light, time runs slow. From our point of view, the muon's internal clock is barely ticking. A trip that should take several of its lifetimes takes only a fraction of one.
The muons weren't breaking the rules. They were living in a different time than we are.
But muons are exotic — tiny, fast, far away. What about something ordinary? Like a clock… on a plane.
In October 1971, a physicist named Joseph Hafele and an astronomer from the U.S. Naval Observatory, Richard Keating, did something that sounds like a joke.
They bought plane tickets for atomic clocks.
Four cesium-beam clocks — among the most precise timekeepers of the era — flew on ordinary commercial flights, all the way around the world. First heading east. Then heading west.
Back in Washington, the Naval Observatory's clocks stayed on the ground, ticking as usual.

Einstein's theories predicted two effects pulling in opposite directions. Speed slows time down. Height speeds it up — the weaker the gravity, the faster a clock ticks. And because the Earth itself is spinning, flying east or west changes how fast the clocks are really moving.
When the clocks came home, they no longer agreed with the ones that stayed behind.
The eastbound clocks had lost about 59 billionths of a second. The westbound clocks had gained about 273.
The predictions? A loss of about 40, and a gain of about 275 — agreement within the uncertainties of the experiment.
Two trips around the planet. A few hundred billionths of a second. And Einstein was right again.

Today, this isn't just a curiosity. GPS satellites orbit about twenty thousand kilometers up, and their clocks run faster than ours by about thirty-eight millionths of a second every day. Leave that uncorrected, and your phone's map would drift by kilometers within a single day.
But a plane still flies ten kilometers high. How small can the difference get — and still be measured?
In 2010, physicists at the National Institute of Standards and Technology, in Boulder, Colorado, had built something far better than a cesium clock.

Their clocks ticked using a single aluminum ion — one electrically charged atom, held in place by electric fields and read out with lasers. The best of them kept time to within one second in about 3.7 billion years.
So they took two of these clocks, and asked a very small question.
They raised one of them by 33 centimeters. About a foot. Roughly two steps on a staircase.
And the higher clock ran faster.
Not by much. Over a 79-year lifetime, that difference adds up to about 90 billionths of a second.
But it's measurable. Every time you climb the stairs, you age a tiny bit faster. Every time you lie down, your head and your feet fall back in step.
They tested the other half of Einstein's idea too. They set one ion moving back and forth at just a few meters per second — about the speed of a jog — and that clock ticked slower.
Time bends with height. Time bends with speed. Even at human scale.
But thirty-three centimeters still wasn't the limit.
In 2022, a team led by physicist Jun Ye at JILA — a joint institute of NIST and the University of Colorado Boulder — pushed the question to its extreme.
They didn't compare two clocks. They used one cloud.

About a hundred thousand strontium atoms, trapped in a vacuum chamber and cooled to a tiny fraction of a degree above absolute zero. Laser light stacks them into thin layers — like a stack of pancakes made of light — and every atom in the stack becomes a clock.
The whole stack is about a millimeter tall. Roughly the width of a sharp pencil tip.
Then they compared the ticking at the top of the cloud with the ticking at the bottom.
And the top was ticking faster.

Across one millimeter, the difference in rate is about one part in ten billion billion. To see it, the team compared frequencies with an uncertainty of just 7.6 parts in a thousand billion billion. If a clock were that precise, it would drift less than a hundredth of a second over the entire age of the universe.

And they didn't just catch the effect once. They saw it as a smooth gradient — tick rates changing steadily from the bottom of the cloud to the top — exactly as Einstein's general relativity predicts.
Our best clocks are now so sensitive that they can feel time change across something smaller than a grain of sand.
So here is where four experiments leave us.
There is no single time. No master clock ticking for the whole universe. Every place has its own time — a little faster where gravity is weaker, a little slower where you're moving faster.
A particle racing down a mountain. Clocks with plane tickets. Two stair steps. A cloud one millimeter tall.
Time isn't the background of the universe. It's part of the landscape — and it bends.
And right now, as you watch this, the top of your head is getting older than your feet.
Not by much. But it is.
